steps: Plan the installation
Plan the fireplace, chimney and options together. Avoid cutting roof and floor joists and keep the chimney inside the house where you can; no special floor reinforcement is needed.

• Note the roof and floor joists and pick a spot that doesn't require cutting them.
  • Run the chimney up inside the house if possible. Outside, enclose it in an insulated chase; a cold chimney causes poor draft.
  • Clean Face: allow an extra 12" on the left to connect the intake air duct. Heat Dump option: an extra 12" on the chosen side.
  • Many options need wiring or electricity. Run it during framing if they might ever be added.

Figure 9 (p. 17) shows Louvered framing examples as a drawing only; its framing dimensions are larger than required, for ease of installation. The general layouts are Figures 10 (Louvered) and 11 (Clean Face) on pp. 18-19.
Install the top standoff

Before installing the fireplace, make sure the back shield is open on the back side (Figure 12), then fit the supplied standoff to the top with the screws from the manual bag. Don't fill the gap between fireplace and standoff with insulation or anything else.
Secure it to the floor
The fireplace must be attached to the floor: refit the four small crate brackets around the base, with at least one screwed into a floor joist (2" wood screws) if possible.
Frame the enclosure
Any suitable framing. Combustibles no closer than the standoffs (0") at top, back and sides, and no combustible framing directly above the unit except facing and mantel supports.

Combustibles to standoffs0"
Ceiling height, sealed enclosure7' min
Ceiling height, vented enclosure6' min
Vented enclosure grilles3"x10" or larger, within 1' of floor and ceiling

Ceiling height is measured from the base of the fireplace to the lowest point of the ceiling, and the ceiling firestop must never be closer than that. Studs (2x4 or 2x6), plywood and gypsum board are all acceptable for the enclosure walls.

Keep the space directly above the fireplace free of combustibles up to the Table 1 (C) height, except framing that supports the facing and mantel. Don't pack required air spaces with insulation.
Connect outside air
Insulated aluminium flex duct rated over 200° F: 4" for total runs under 25', 5" for longer. Max 12' vertical rise; the inlet sits at least 5' below the rain cap, never in an attic.

1. Pick a spot for the duct and inlet; the inlet can be above or below floor level.
  2. Cut a 4 ¼" hole (5 ¼" for 5" duct) in the outside wall, push the inlet in from outside and seal the joint.
  3. Pull back the insulation and cover at both ends, screw the duct to the inlet and to the fireplace sleeve, then pull the insulation back and tape the cover with 2" aluminium duct tape.

Both 4" and 5" sleeves are supplied. Looping the duct makes an optional cold air trap. Don't crimp the duct at corners.
Install the EXCEL chimney
7" ICC EXCEL only, 12' to 40' from the fireplace top to below the rain cap. Frame 13" square openings, keep 2" to combustibles and fit a radiation shield at every floor.

1. Frame 13" square holes in floors, ceilings and roof (up to 13 ½", never smaller).
  2. From below, install a radiation shield at each floor; at the attic, a radiation shield and a storm collar.
  3. Remove the flue adapter, screw it to the first chimney length, refit it on the fireplace, then assemble the chimney.
  4. Fit the roof radiation shield (XM-7ERRS) so it extends 1" above the roof line.
  5. Flashing: vented if the chimney is enclosed to the roof, regular if not. Seal it with roofing tar (on sloped roofs, under the upper shingles and over the lower ones) and nail it down.
  6. Seal the storm collar with silicone (not roofing tar), then fit and secure the rain cap.

Terminate at least 3' above the roof contact and 2' higher than anything within 10'. More than 5' above the roof needs a roof brace. The fireplace supports up to 18' of chimney; follow the EXCEL manual for supports and bracing. Don't fill the 2" clearance with insulation.
Offsets, chase or masonry
Offsets: max 30° in the USA (45° in Canada), four elbows max, 3 metal screws per joint and a support above each offset. A masonry chimney still needs EXCEL from the fireplace plus a listed liner.

Offsets

An elbow can sit directly on the fireplace. Secure every joint with 3 metal screws, return to vertical with a second elbow, and add a wall or offset support above each offset; elbows don't carry the chimney. Through an exterior wall, use an angled wall insulated radiation shield (XM-7EWRSI30 or XM-7EWRSI45).

Chase

Build it as an extension of the home and insulate it: to the first firestop in mild climates, to the top in very cold ones, plus the chase ceiling.

Masonry

  • Run EXCEL from the fireplace to the wall, then a listed stainless liner (ULC-S635, ULC-S640 or UL-1777) inside the clay liner to the top.
  • Join them with masonry adaptor FO-FDM7 (3 rivets to the liner, 3 screws to the EXCEL).
  • Use at least one 18" EXCEL length after the elbow; where the EXCEL enters the masonry it must be at least 12" from the ceiling.
  • Under 10"x10" inside, a listed stainless flexible liner with adaptor LM-7LAF can be used.
  • An existing chimney must first be inspected by the authority having jurisdiction, and serve only this fireplace.
Finish the facing

Facing must be non-combustible (brick, slate, ceramic tile). Gypsum board isn't acceptable and must stay behind the side standoffs and the Table 1 (L) top clearance. A Clean Face needs its intake duct and two gravity vent kits.

• Thin materials (tile, sliced brick) can go on the FO-KP3 rock retainer kit, or be glued to the face with high-temperature silicone.
  • Clean Face (FO-F3): you must install its intake duct and two Gravity Vent Kits (FO-V2 or FO-V3). Skipping either overheats the unit. Gravity vent dampers can't be used on a Clean Face, and electrical options inside it will be hard to reach later.
  • Louvered with the upper louver blocked off: two Gravity Vent Kits are also required, with no gravity vent dampers.
  • Each gravity vent kit has 5' of insulated flexible duct; add 5' lengths (FO-DUCT5) up to 15' max.
  • Use only genuine RSF parts; substitutes decertify the system.
Note: For the non-combustible zone above the fireplace, Table 1 (L) on p. 8 gives 39 ¼" from the firebox opening to combustible wall materials; the warning label in Figures 10 and 11 (pp. 18-19) says the wall surface directly above the fireplace must be non-combustible for 18".
Hearth extension & spark guard

Non-combustible hearth extension at least 18" deep and 42" wide, centered on the opening; no minimum thickness. Fit the supplied 5" x 36" spark guard halfway under the unit (not needed on a non-combustible floor).

The spark guard sits halfway under the fireplace and halfway under the hearth extension, centered on the door opening, reaching 2½" beneath the fireplace.

Raised installation: a custom Z-shaped guard if the base is 2 ½" or less above the hearth flooring, or a right-angle guard (sides at least 2½" x 2½", covered with non-combustible material) if it is higher. Custom guards aren't supplied.
Mantel
Combustible shelf up to 12" deep, 32" to 36 ½" above the firebox opening depending on depth (Table 2). Side posts must be non-combustible unless they meet the 16" side wall clearance.

panels.title: Smoke comes in when the door opens
items: Door opened too quickly → open it more slowly
Dirty chimney or plugged cap → clean it; screened caps clog with creosote
Chimney too short → check height for altitude and elbows (Table 3)
Central heat or internal blower running → turn it off first
Range hood or bathroom fan running → open a window near the fireplace a little
Too little kindling → smoke is most likely while lighting

panels.title: Burns too fast, can't slow it down
items: Air leaking past door seals or gaskets → check them with the paper test
Poorly adjusted door(s) → over-firing, excess wood use, early catalyst failure
Excessive draft → hotter fire, shorter burn times
Chimney connector behind the top louver glows red → over-firing

panels.title: Less heat than it used to give
items: Catalyst may need cleaning or replacement
Not glowing red in a hot fire with the bypass closed → it isn't firing
Not firing for several days, even in hot fires → replace it (FO-CATP)
Bypass closed before the fireplace was hot → dirty catalyst, no extra heat
Wet wood → lots of wood burned for very little heat

panels.title: Hard to light or smoky (weak draft)
items: Weak draft → smoke in the room, hard lighting; adding chimney height is the most common fix
Cold chimney outside the house → enclose it in an insulated chase
Unseasoned, wet wood → excess visible smoke and poor burning
Severely depressurized house → outside air won't stop the smoking

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
1. Open the bypass: pull the bypass handle all the way out.
  2. Open the air: move the air control lever, below the door on the right, all the way right.
  3. Lay the fire: crumpled newspaper, enough to light the kindling (5-6 pieces should do), with plenty of kindling crisscrossed on top. Never use flammable liquids.
  4. Light the paper and close the door most of the way, but not completely. You should see air rushing in.
  5. Add wood: once the kindling is burning, add at least 3 small pieces of seasoned wood. Use the andirons so you don't smother the fire.
  6. Close the door once the wood is lit. If the fire goes out, you closed it too early.
  7. Engage the catalyst when the fire is hot, after about 15-30 minutes.
No grate. Don't raise the fire. Keep it behind the andirons, and move logs that fall against the glass.
Note: The safety list on p. 3 says to run the fireplace with the door(s) fully closed, since a partly open door can draw gas and flame out. The lighting steps on p. 11 say to leave the door slightly open until the wood is lit.

The first few fires

Expect a slow start. The firebricks stay black until a few hot fires dry them out, then turn white. A slight odor from curing paint is normal and may set off a smoke detector, so open doors and windows. No small break-in fires are needed.

catalyst.title: Engaging the catalyst
catalyst.html:
The catalyst burns off smoke, so you get more heat and a cleaner burn. The bypass handle switches it in and out.

  1. Light the fire with the bypass open (handle pulled all the way out).
  2. When the fire is hot, usually after 15 to 30 minutes, push the handle all the way in. That closes the bypass and sends the smoke through the catalyst.
Not too early. The catalyst must reach at least 175°C (350°F) to work. Engage it before the fireplace is hot and it gets dirty and gives no extra heat.

Reading the probe

A probe measures the temperature within 1" of the catalyst. Plug the optional FO-DTD display or any Type K thermometer into the connector on the left side, inside the casing. Read it with the bypass closed.

Below 175°C (350°F)Add wood, open the air, keep the bypass open
175°C to 700°C (350°F to 1300°F)Just right; keep the bypass closed except to reload
Above 700°C (1300°F)Add no wood, close the air, let the fire die down

Care

Check it at least three times a heating season. Brush ash off the cold catalyst with a soft brush. If it won't glow red in a hot fire with the bypass closed for several days, replace it (kit FO-CATP). It lasts about 5-10 years, and each overheating shortens that.

air.title: Setting the burn rate
air.html:
There's no flue damper. Closing the door seals the fireplace, and the air control lever (front, right, below the door) sets how much air the fire gets.

All the way rightFully open: the most air
Toward the leftLess air: a slower fire and a longer burn

Finding the right setting

  • For the first few days, burn with the lever fully open while you learn the fireplace.
  • Then close it a little at a time. If the fire doesn't change, you can close it more. If it smolders or goes out, it needs more air.
  • Always keep visible flames in the firebox.
  • A hot fireplace needs less lever movement: a built-in bimetal damper already closes the air part way as it heats up.
  • A fast fire gives more heat, but it burns much more wood and sends more heat up the chimney.

Outside or room air

A sliding door behind the bottom louver, below the firebox, picks the air source. Push it back for outside air, or pull it forward for room air. Outside air helps the fire start.

Don't tamper with the factory air control or try to lower the minimum burn rate. It's against federal regulations.

reload.title: Adding wood
reload.html:
1. Get the wood ready first. The catalyst cools fast while the door is open, but don't rush.
  2. Open the bypass: pull the handle all the way out. Turn off the central heat or internal blower if you have one; a running blower can push smoke out of the fireplace.
  3. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill into the room.
  4. Stir and load. Poke and stir the unburnt wood to revive the fire, then add the new logs. Keep a clear path in front of the pilot, the metal tube centered between the two andiron posts. It feeds air to the coals.
  5. Leave the door slightly ajar for about 3-10 minutes, until the new wood is well lit, then close it.
  6. Close the bypass (push the handle in) once the wood is well lit.
Smoke when you open the door? Check that kitchen and bathroom fans are off. They can pull smoke out of the fireplace.
Note: The safety list on p. 3 says to run the fireplace with the door(s) fully closed, since a partly open door can draw gas and flame out. The refueling steps on p. 12 say to keep the door slightly ajar for about 3-10 minutes.

fuel.title: What wood to burn
fuel.html:
Burn seasoned firewood: wood that has been cut, split and dried under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more. Dry seasoned wood generally has less than 20% moisture.

  • Wet wood is hard to burn, gives very little heat, builds creosote and leaves dark deposits on the glass.
  • Hardwoods burn longer and more evenly, because more weight fits in the firebox.
  • Densified fuel logs are fine, on their own or mixed with wood.
  • Wax fire logs (like Duraflame) aren't recommended because they dirty the glass. If you use them, burn only one at a time and don't poke or stir it. Use only fire logs evaluated for fireplace use.
Never burn driftwood, treated wood, coal, garbage, plastic or scrap. Don't use construction scraps (2x4 or plywood) as your only fuel. Large amounts of paper, cardboard or mill ends can over-fire and damage the fireplace, or start a chimney fire if the flue is dirty.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Some deposits on the glass are normal: a controlled fire isn't always hot enough to keep it perfectly clean. A good hot fire once a day usually burns most of them off. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

When you clean it

  • Wait until the glass is cool. Cleaning hot glass can cause a serious burn.
  • Use only a cleaner your dealer recommends. Wood stove glass cleaners work far better than regular glass or oven cleaners.
  • Never use an abrasive cleaner.
  • Heat won't break the glass, but an impact can. Don't hit it, and don't slam the door.
Keep glass cleaner off the paint. It may strip the finish. Clean painted and plated parts with a soft damp cloth, mild detergent and water.

Worn spots on the black face can be touched up with Stove Bright Metallic Black high-temperature paint, never while the fireplace is still warm.

chimney.title: Chimney, creosote & ashes
chimney.html:
A slow fire gives off tar and vapors that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If it catches fire, it burns extremely hot.

Check and sweep the chimney

  • Check for creosote every week or so, until you learn how often your chimney needs cleaning.
  • Clean it at 1/8" (3mm) of buildup or more.
  • Soot or creosote more than 1/8" (3mm) thick means the chimney needs cleaning immediately (p. 4). That may also mean changing how you burn and checking more often.
  • Before sweeping, close the door(s) and open the bypass. Use a 7" round brush.
  • Afterwards, vacuum out any creosote or ash that fell into the top of the fireplace, through the bypass opening, with a flexible attachment.
  • Never use chemical chimney cleaners. They can ruin the catalyst.

Ashes

Remove ashes before they're deep enough to spill out when you open the door. Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, on a non-combustible floor or the ground, well away from anything that burns. Keep them in the closed container until every cinder is cold. With a lower louver, the optional ash pan kit (FO-AP) makes this easier.

door.title: Door seal & adjustment
door.html:
A good door seal is the most important part of controlling the burn. A poor seal can mean lower efficiency, over-firing, more wood used and early catalyst failure.

Check the seal

Close a thin sheet of paper in the door and latch it. Pull gently but firmly. If the paper tears or is hard to pull out, the seal is good. Repeat all around the door(s). Worn or damaged gaskets should be replaced; kits come from your RSF dealer.

Your model's doors

Opel 2 Plus (OPEL+ 2C)Double doors; latch and hinges adjust
Opel 3 Plus (OPEL+ 3C)Single door; hinge adjusts, progressive latch
  • Double doors: it's normal to push on the handle to close them. Grease the latch and hinges at least once a year with the high-temperature grease provided.
  • Single door: the more you turn the handle, the tighter the seal on the right side. Don't always over-tighten it; that wears out the gasket early.

The adjustment steps are on p. 15 (double doors) and p. 16 (single door).

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• Keep furniture, firewood and anything else that burns at least 4' from the front of the fireplace.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of your home, and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Keep them well away while the fireplace is in use.
  • Don't use a grate or any product not specified for this fireplace.
  • Don't slam the door; the glass can break.
  • Never run it with the catalyst removed or deactivated. That's against the law.
  • Don't burn chemical chimney cleaners.
Signs of over-firing: you can't slow the fire down, or the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red. Don't over-fire the fireplace. If it burns too fast, check the door seals and gaskets for air leaks.

Burning wood makes carbon monoxide. Keep the door gasket sealing and the chimney joints in good shape.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF warrants its fireplaces against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, on these terms:

First yearDefective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Second to fifth yearsParts repaired or replaced; no labor
Sixth to thirtieth yearsReplacement parts, if available, at 50% of retail; no labor
Electrical componentsOne year only
Catalytic combustor5 years: no charge the first 2 years, then you pay 60%, 70% and 80% of retail in years 3, 4 and 5

Not covered

  • Glass and plating
  • Normal wear, such as paint discoloration, worn gaskets, eroded or cracked refractory
  • Vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or loads, or skipped service
  • An installation that doesn't follow the manual, and damage in transit
The warranty isn't transferable. A failed catalyst goes back to your dealer with a Combustor Failure Report and your original proof of purchase.

specOutput.title: Emissions, efficiency & output
specOutput.html:
Emission rate0.7 grams per hour (2020 U.S. EPA particulate standard, crib wood)
Overall efficiency70% (higher heating value)
Maker's website: Optimal Efficiency 80% (Low Heating Value/LHV, CSA B415.1-10); EPA Average Efficiency 70% (High Heating Value/HHV, CSA B415.1-10).
Maximum heat output27 034 BTU/hr
Maker's website: BTU Output 27,034 BTU/hr (EPA certification testing with crib wood, CSA B415.1-10); Estimated BTU Potential 70,000 BTU/hr (engineering calculations).
CombustionCatalytic combustor with bypass

Lab results from a crib wood EPA emission test using CSA B415.1-10 calculations; the manual notes that output varies with the installation, chimney height and wood. Combustion air comes only through the draft control: a bimetal coil plus a manual lever (or an optional electric wall thermostat).

The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory and must not be altered. Don't install a flue damper to slow it. Operating with the catalyst deactivated or removed is against federal regulations.

specChimney.title: Chimney
specChimney.html:
Chimney7" ICC Model EXCEL only
Min / max height12' / 40' (fireplace top to below the rain cap)
Max height supported by the fireplace18'
Max offset angle30° (USA) · 45° (Canada)
Max elbowsFour (two offsets and returns)
Clearance to combustibles2" or more, no insulation
Rough opening13" square (up to 13 ½", never smaller)
Above the roof3' above the contact point; 2' higher than anything within 10'

Raise the minimum height by about 6" for every 1000' of elevation, and for every offset; Table 3 on p. 21 gives the recommended flue heights. The manual's example: at 6015', at least 15' straight, or 18'6" with one 30° offset. More than 5' above the roof needs a roof brace.

specClear.title: Clearances
specClear.html:
Combustibles to side, back and top standoffs0"
Side wall to side of firebox opening16" min
Ceiling height, sealed enclosure7' min
Ceiling height, vented enclosure6' min
Combustible wall materials above the facing39 ¼" min from the firebox opening
Chimney to combustibles2" or more

Ceiling height runs from the base of the fireplace to the lowest point of the ceiling, inside and outside the enclosure. A vented enclosure needs 3"x10" or larger grilles within 1' of both the floor and the ceiling. Figure 1 (p. 7) labels 7 1/8" from the side standoff to the side of the firebox opening and 26 3/8" from the base to the top of the opening; the other unit dimensions appear only on that drawing.

Note: For the non-combustible zone above the fireplace, Table 1 (L) on p. 8 gives 39 ¼" from the firebox opening to combustible wall materials; the warning label in Figures 10 and 11 (pp. 18-19) says the wall surface directly above the fireplace must be non-combustible for 18".

specMantel.title: Combustible mantel
specMantel.html:
Minimum height from the highest point of the firebox opening to the underside of a combustible mantel (Table 2):

0" to 4" deep32"
6" deep33 1/8"
8" deep34 ¼"
10" deep35 3/8"
12" deep (max)36 ½"

Interpolate between the two nearest depths; the manual's example puts a 9 ¼" mantel at 35". For a variable-depth profile, neither its widest part nor its lowest point may sit below the height for its depth. No combustible mantel goes lower than 32". Side posts must be non-combustible unless they meet the 16" side wall clearance (Table 1 B). Masonry or other non-combustible mantels can go anywhere on the facing, as long as they don't block the louvers.

Table 1 (J) on p. 8 gives 12" as the maximum mantel depth. The text on p. 9 states the same limit when it says a combustible mantel cannot be wider than 12": there, as in its rule for variable-depth profiles, wide means depth.

specHearth.title: Hearth extension & spark guard
specHearth.html:
Depth, from the front of the fireplace18" min
Total width, centered on the firebox opening42" min
ThicknessNo minimum
Spark guard width36" min

Use non-combustible material such as brick, tile, stone or slate. Install the supplied spark guard (a 5" x 36" piece of sheet metal) halfway under the fireplace and halfway under the hearth extension, centered on the door opening, so it reaches 2½" beneath the fireplace. It isn't needed on a non-combustible floor.

Raised installations

  • Base 2 ½" or less above the hearth flooring: a Z-shaped spark guard as tall as that gap, reaching at least 2½" under both the hearth extension and the fireplace.
  • More than 2 ½": a right-angle spark guard with sides of at least 2½" x 2½", covered with non-combustible material.

Custom spark guards aren't supplied. They need the 36" minimum width and must be centered on the door opening.

specAir.title: Outside air
specAir.html:
DuctInsulated aluminium flexible duct rated over 200° F
Diameter4" if the total run is under 25'; 5" for longer runs
Maker's website: Outside Air 4", meets R2000 / 5" also acceptable / can operate with room air. Install to the manual.
Wall hole4 ¼" (5 ¼" for 5" duct)
Vertical rise12' max above the base of the unit
Inlet locationAt least 5' below the chimney rain cap; never in an attic

Both 4" and 5" connecting sleeves come with the fireplace. The inlet can be above or below floor level. Seal the inlet to the wall, screw the bare duct to the inlet and to the fireplace sleeve, then pull the insulation back over and tape the cover with 2" aluminium duct tape. A loop in the duct makes an optional cold air trap. Don't crimp the duct at corners. A Clean Face unit needs an extra 12" on the left to connect its intake duct.

The owner picks outside or room air with the sliding door behind the bottom louver.

specGas.title: Gas log conversion
specGas.html:
The fireplace can take a vented gas log as long as the air control lever stays fully open (to the right) and the bypass stays open at all times.

Max gas output35,000 BTU
Log set listingANSI Z21.60/CSA 2.26
Gas line entry1 ½" hole on either side, about 9" up from the bottom
ClearancesNone required from the firebox; the log maker's apply
  1. Remove and keep the round central refractory brick, the two bottom bricks and the central plug (locknut, bolt, top and bottom plates, reached through the bottom louver). They all go back in to burn wood again.
  2. Remove the side firebrick on the gas side, drill through the side of the firebox, and drill or break a hole in that brick for the line.
  3. Leave the ash pan hole completely open; it brings air to the gas log.
  4. Install the log per its maker's instructions. The valve may go inside the firebox if the log maker allows it.
Not tested with unvented gas logs: never install one. Don't install a gas log lighter; the fireplace's heat will permanently damage it. Gas line work by qualified personnel, to local codes.

specModels.title: Models covered
specModels.html:
The manual (OPEL PLUS 2C - 3C) covers both models with one set of specifications, clearances, chimney and hearth requirements. They differ only in the door.

Opel 2 Plus = OPEL+ 2CDouble doors; Allen-key latch and hinge-nut adjustment (p. 15)
Opel 3 Plus = OPEL+ 3CSingle door, progressive latch; hinge-screw adjustment (p. 16)

Either can be Louvered (FO-OPLB black or FO-OPLC decorative black louvers) or Clean Face (FO-F3). Figure 1 shows the OPEL2C with decorative grills and the OPEL3C with regular louvers; the unit dimensions appear only on that drawing.

The listing label is glued to the bottom of the fireplace, below the floor shield: remove the bottom louver to see it (p. 29). For replacement parts, the manual says to contact your RSF dealer.

Same door-position conflict for reloading: p. 3 item 3 vs the refueling section (p. 12), which says to keep the door slightly ajar for about 3-10 minutes after loading.

Non-combustible zone above the fireplace: Table 1 (L) gives 39 ¼" from the firebox opening to combustible wall materials (p. 8); the warning label in Figures 10 and 11 says the wall surface directly above the fireplace must be non-combustible for 18" (pp. 18-19).
